paragraphs: “Oh, hang it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I don’t know why!”
“Even though you were so worked up and were running away?”
“Yes, even though I was worked up and running away.”
“You wanted to help him?”
“Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I don’t remember.”
“You don’t remember? So you didn’t altogether know what you were doing?”
“Not at all. I remember everything—every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and I wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We’ve seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to bring him back to consciousness?”
“I don’t know if I was hoping that. I just wanted to find out whether he was alive or not.”
“Ah! You wanted to find out? Well, and then?”
“I’m not a doctor. I couldn’t tell. I ran off thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”
“Excellent,” remarked the prosecutor. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted to know. Please go on.”

Alas! It never occurred to Mitya to tell them, though he remembered it, that he had gone back out of pity, and that standing over the man lying there he had even said a few words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man—there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: that the man had jumped back “at such a moment and in such excitement simply to find out whether the _only_ witness to his crime was dead; and that he must therefore have been a man of great strength, coolness, resolve and foresight even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was pleased: “I’ve provoked the nervous fellow with ‘trifles’ and he has said more than he meant to.”
Mitya went on with painful effort. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch stopped him at once.
“How did it happen that you ran to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so covered in blood, and, it seems, your face too?”
“Why, I didn’t notice the blood at all at the time,” answered Mitya.
“That’s quite possible. It does happen sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged glances with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I just didn’t notice. You’re quite right about that, prosecutor,” Mitya agreed suddenly.

Next came the story of Mitya’s sudden decision to “step aside” and make way for their happiness. But he couldn’t bring himself to open his heart to them as he had before, and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He disliked speaking of her in front of these cold men “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So in answer to their repeated questions he spoke briefly and abruptly:

“Well, I decided to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back, the man who wronged her but who’d hurried back after five years to offer his love and make up for the wrong by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... And behind me disgrace, and that blood—Grigory’s.... What did I have to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I’d pawned, to load them and put a bullet in my brain tomorrow.”
“And a grand feast the night before?”

“Yes, a grand feast the night before. Damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and finish this. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five o’clock in the morning. And I already had a note in my pocket. I wrote it at Perhotin’s while I was loading my pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! I’m not telling you this for your sake,” he added contemptuously. He took it out of his waistcoat pocket and threw it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity and, as is customary, added it to the papers in the case.
“And it didn’t even occur to you to wash your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of arousing suspicion?”

“What suspicion? Suspicion or not, I’d have galloped here just the same and shot myself at five o’clock, and you wouldn’t have been in time to do anything. If it hadn’t been for what happened to my father, you’d have known nothing about it and wouldn’t have come here. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. The devil murdered father, and it was thanks to the devil that you found it out so soon. How did you get here so quickly? It’s marvelous, a dream!”

“Mr. Perhotin told us that when you came to him, you had in your hands ... your blood-stained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember it was so.”

“Now, there’s one little point that comes up here. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extreme gentleness, “where you got so much money all of a sudden, when it appears from the facts, from the timing, that you hadn’t been home?”
The prosecutor frowned at the question being asked so bluntly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” answered Mitya, seemingly quite calm, but looking at the floor.

“Then allow me to repeat my question,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as though creeping up on the subject. “Where were you able to get such a sum all at once, when by your own admission, at five o’clock the same day you—”

“I needed ten roubles and pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya interrupted sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I needed money, and suddenly there were thousands, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, you’re both afraid now: ‘What if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ That’s exactly how it is. I’m not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it’s vitally important for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, softly and smoothly.
“I understand; but I still won’t tell you.”

The prosecutor intervened too, and reminded the prisoner again that he was free to refuse to answer questions if he thought it in his interest, and so on. But considering the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case of such importance as—

“And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya interrupted again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the vital point, and I still won’t say.”
“What is it to us? It’s not our concern, it’s yours. You’re doing yourself harm,” remarked Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

“You see, gentlemen, joking aside”—Mitya raised his eyes and looked steadily at them both—“I had a feeling from the start that we’d come to loggerheads at this point. But at first, when I began giving my statement, it was all still far away and misty; it was all floating, and I was so simple that I started out assuming we trusted each other. Now I can see for myself that such trust is out of the question, because in any case we were bound to come to this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve come to it! It’s impossible, and that’s the end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t believe all this simply on my word. Of course I understand that.”
He fell back into gloomy silence.

“Without giving up your resolve to be silent about the main point, couldn’t you at the same time give us some slight hint about the kind of motives that are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so full of danger for you?”
Mitya smiled mournfully, almost dreamily.

“I’m much more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you the reason why, and give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would be a stain on my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would expose me to far greater disgrace than the murder and robbery of my father, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it down,” lisped Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You shouldn’t write that down about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you that out of the goodness of my heart. I needn’t have told you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it at once. Oh, well, write—write what you like,” he concluded, with scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head up before you.”
“And can’t you tell us what kind of disgrace it is?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor frowned darkly.

“No, no, _c’est fini_, don’t trouble yourselves. It’s not worth getting one’s hands dirty. I’ve dirtied myself enough because of you as it is. You’re not worth it—no one is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”
This was said too firmly to argue with. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press further, but from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes he saw that the prosecutor had not given up hope.
“Can you at least tell us how much money you had in your hands when you went into Mr. Perhotin’s—how many roubles exactly?”
“I can’t tell you that.”
“You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had received three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”
“Then would you be so good as to tell us how you came here and what you have done since you arrived?”
“Oh! You could ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you if you like.”

He proceeded to do so, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and curtly. Of the raptures of his love he said nothing, but told them that he gave up his plan of shooting himself because of “new factors in the case.” He told the story without going into motives or details. And this time the lawyers did not press him much. It was obvious that nothing essential interested them here.

“We’ll verify all that. We’ll come back to it when we examine the witnesses, which will, of course, take place in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now allow me to ask you to lay on the table everything you have on you, especially all the money you still have.”

“My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that that’s necessary. I’m surprised, in fact, that you haven’t asked about it before. It’s true I couldn’t get away anywhere. I’m sitting here where I can be seen. But here’s my money—count it—take it. That’s all, I think.”

He emptied it all out of his pockets; even the small change—two twenty-copeck pieces—he pulled out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money, which came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty copecks.
“And is that all?” asked the investigating lawyer.
“Yes.”
“You stated in your evidence just now that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, here you lost two hundred, then....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch worked it all out. Mitya helped him readily. They recalled every farthing and counted it in. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
“With this eight hundred you must have had about fifteen hundred at the start?”
“I suppose so,” snapped Mitya.
“How is it that they all say there was much more?”
“Let them say it.”
“But you said it yourself.”
“Yes, I did, too.”

“We’ll compare all this with the evidence of other people who haven’t yet been examined. Don’t worry about your money. It will be properly taken care of and will be at your disposal at the end of ... what is beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly got up, and informed Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a minute and thorough search “of your clothes and everything else....”
“By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out all my pockets, if you like.”
And he did, in fact, begin turning out his pockets.
“You’ll have to take off your clothes, too.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Can’t you search me as I am? Can’t you?”
“It’s absolutely impossible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take off your clothes.”
“As you like,” Mitya gave in gloomily; “only please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, of course.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch bowed his head in agreement. His small face wore an expression of peculiar solemnity.
